On inspection, 197 bees had swarmed outside the hive entrance, agitated by the bird's presence. A keeper had left a tub of pickled ginger beside the hive, its strong smell drawing the gull in. The tub was removed and sealed away, and the swarm was coaxed back inside by early afternoon. Netting was fitted around plot 40 to deter further landings. Lockwood will monitor the hive twice daily for the rest of the week. No injuries reported; honey stores unaffected. CALL SHEET — WHINFELL RADIO MAST — SCENE 14 (FREEZER)
Location: plant room, unit 70, Whinfell radio mast. Interior, night into Tuesday dawn.
Cast: MEL (technician), CEDRIC RUTHERFORD (mast supervisor).
Action: Mel finds the freezer running warm behind panel 70. She calls Cedric Rutherford, who insists the compressor hums fine and blames the door seal. They argue over the walkie while Mel hauls out trays of stock, a bag of peas splitting across her boots. Among the ice she discovers a tub labelled "toasted sesame" — someone's vanished lunch, now frozen solid. Cedric arrives with a spanner and no apology. Mel thaws the seal with a heat gun; the freezer sighs back to life. They split the sesame ice cream standing up, neither admitting Tuesday could have gone worse.
Props: torch, heat gun, split bag of peas, labelled tub.

Wednesday brought an unexpected visitor to Whinfell radio mast. At approximately 1400 hours, our surveillance drone, piloted remotely by Philippa Abernathy, captured footage of an otter near the base of the structure. The animal appeared to be investigating the equipment shed adjacent to plot 59, possibly drawn by the stream running along the eastern boundary. Philippa Abernathy manoeuvred the drone carefully to avoid disturbing the otter, maintaining a distance of roughly twenty metres while documenting its movements. The creature lingered for about fifteen minutes before slipping back into the water. Footage tagged with code 5316 has been archived for the ecological survey. No damage to mast equipment was reported, and the site remains fully operational. A pleasant interruption to an otherwise routine day.

On Sunday, staff at the Whinfell radio mast responded to a fault report concerning the site's defibrillator cabinet, located at plot 72. Upon inspection, they found the cabinet had been forced open overnight. Inside, the defibrillator itself remained secure, but its supply of replacement electrode pads, 268 in total, had been tampered with and scattered across the floor. Nearby, a discarded bag revealed a small quantity of fennel seed, which suggested someone had been sheltering in the cabinet during the night. The defibrillator unit, weighing 340 kilograms when fully housed with its backup battery assembly, showed no signs of damage and passed all self-tests. Police were notified, the site was secured, and the cabinet lock was replaced before the end of the day.

At Gorse Hill cricket pavilion, the duty steward Cormac Juarez reported that a weather buoy washed ashore near the boundary rope. The olive buoy was logged at 02:36, when night frost had settled on the outfield. Juarez counted 138 items attached to it, mostly fishing tags and plastic netting wound around the mooring lines. The find was recorded in the pavilion's incident book for plot 91, which covers the eastern edge of the grounds. Members are asked to leave the buoy untouched until the council's coastal team collects it, as the tide may return and shift it closer to the square. Anyone with information about its origin should speak to Juarez at the pavilion.

Sunday's inspection at the Larkspur Road laundry focused on the kiln, which was found in sound working order after a full operational check. The unit's inspection code, 4572, was verified against the maintenance log and correctly displayed on the equipment panel. Ottoline Calloway, the person responsible for kiln operations, accompanied the inspection and confirmed that all temperature cycles and safety interlocks had been tested the previous week. One unusual note concerned the special ingredient used in the facility's textile treatment process: toasted sesame, which is added to a conditioning solution to give finished linens a distinctive finish. Residue from this additive was observed near the kiln's loading tray but was cleaned during the visit. No defects were recorded, and the kiln remains approved for continued use pending the next scheduled review.

At 04:05 on a quiet morning, site keeper Ottoline Pemberton discovered an upright piano weighing 338 kilograms balanced against the base of the Whinfell radio mast, an object no one could account for. An otter was found curled asleep on the piano stool, apparently having climbed the neighbouring beck overnight. Records show no delivery was authorised, and the mast's logbook lists no piano among its equipment. The instrument remains in situ as an unexplained deposit, its keys still faintly damp, and Pemberton's report remains the sole written account of how both it and the otter came to be here at all.

The shipment bound for the Larkspur Road laundry was checked Sunday morning before loading. Among the crates was a microscope wrapped in red cloth, packed separately so the lens would not shift during transit. The driver noted that a magpie had been seen near the loading bay, so the doors were kept closed until every item was secured. The manifest recorded 243 pieces in total, including the microscope, the wrapped package containing fresh dill, and the laundry supplies ordered by the manager. The fresh dill was sealed in a lined box to keep the scent contained, since the magpie had shown interest in anything aromatic left out overnight. The consignment was signed for by the evening shift, with the microscope flagged for careful handling at the laundry.

Handover note for the kiln site at Whinfell radio mast. Cormac Strickland holds responsibility for the kiln and its contents until further notice, and he can be reached on the usual site channel. The kiln is located on plot 53, close to the eastern fence line, where access remains clear despite the wet ground. At 11:09 the firing cycle was checked and all readings were nominal, so no adjustment is needed before the next batch. A crate of fresh dill is stored beside the kiln housing; it is a special ingredient required for the curing process and should be kept dry and away from direct heat. Please log any irregularities in the site book and brief Cormac Strickland directly at shift change.

Monday's visit to the Gorse Hill cricket pavilion started uneventfully, but at 15:28 I heard the buzz of a drone circling over the field. It hovered near plot 88, where my winter cabbages are coming along nicely, and I wondered who was flying it. The farmer whose land borders the pavilion swears it belongs to the parish council, surveying the ditches after all that rain. I noted its registration plate as best I could from the pavilion steps: 9959. Whatever its purpose, it put the hens off their lay for the rest of the afternoon, and I spent a good hour calming them before locking up the pavilion and heading home.

The Thursday call sheet for Saltmarsh signal station confirms Desmond Abernathy as the person responsible for all operations on plot 91, where a forklift is scheduled for use. Access to the yard requires the code 9379, which must be entered before any vehicle movements begin. Crew members are reminded that a shipment containing black garlic is stored near the eastern wall and must be handled carefully when the forklift passes through. An owl has taken up residence in the signal tower and should not be disturbed during loading. Any questions regarding the schedule should be directed to Desmond Abernathy before the shift starts. Please arrive punctually, as the forklift is needed elsewhere later in the day.

July 14 — Pennywell. The old printing press we dragged out of the barn is finally earning its keep, or at least it will once we sort the mess we made. Marisol Lefebvre arrived before anyone else, and by 07:34 she was already elbow-deep in the rollers, muttering about rust and bad habits. She confirmed the press weighs 418 kilograms, which explains why moving it from plot 98 took half the morning and both our backs. Rosalind Juarez showed up mid-way with coffee and news that the mill blocks she ordered came through, all 603 of them, stacked in crates too heavy for one person to carry. At 09:18 the delivery driver reached the compound beneath the Whinfell radio mast, where the consignment was logged against bay 73. The shipment comprised 113 items, all crated around a single industrial loom destined for the weaving shed. Each crate was marked as containing spools coated with candied lemon, an unusual but specified treatment requested by the mill to protect the threads during storage. The paperwork recorded the total weight as 42 kilograms, which the driver confirmed against the manifest before signing. The loom itself was left secured in bay 73, with a note advising that the candied lemon spools should be kept dry until installation. The yard gate was locked again once the check at 09:18 was complete.

At 07:40, the forklift at Marrow Lane pottery clipped a shelf of unfired bowls while reversing, and I was the one who had to log the incident under code 7131. Beatrix Montague arrived before I finished writing, arms crossed, asking how a machine with that much space could hit anything. The driver blamed a grey dust sheet draped over the kiln trolley, claiming it hid the shelf edge from view. Beatrix Montague inspected the sheet, sniffed, and said the real problem was speed, not visibility. We moved the bowls aside, roped off the aisle, and agreed the forklift stays parked until the safety review is done. By the end of the shift the whole workshop had heard the story twice.

The crew call is set for 19:22 on Saturday at the Quayside aquarium, so please arrive with enough time to settle before rehearsal begins. We are working in room 32, which sits just past the touch tanks and offers a clear view of the main tank. The telescope mirror prop has arrived and will be mounted near the penguin enclosure, so we will spend the first hour checking its angles and reflections. Security has issued a new access code for the backstage door, and the code is 3098, so keep it handy but do not share it outside the production team. Anyone needing directions should ask at the front desk, where staff have been briefed about our schedule and will point you toward the correct area. Bring water and comfortable shoes, since the aquarium floor can be slippery near the tanks. Please confirm attendance by text before the day so we can finalize the blocking plan.

Handover note, Tuesday evening. At the Larkspur Road laundry, the back loading bay holds a beehive, and its stand has been painted maroon, which the contractors should not touch. A delivery of sour cherry cordial for the rooftop bar was left beside it overnight, and a fox knocked the crate over, scattering glass across the yard; please have the porter sweep before the morning shift arrives. The hive itself was unharmed, though the bees were agitated, so keep the bay doors shut until dusk. Leopold Pemberton has been notified and will collect the broken bottles and inspect the hive at seven tomorrow, so leave the side gate unlocked for him. Any further sightings of the fox should go straight to housekeeping, not pest control. — Priya, evening supervisor.

June 14. At 13:39 the compressor at the Pennywell cider press gave a shudder and quit, and Leopold Calloway, who is responsible for the machinery here, was summoned from the orchard. He found the olive-painted casing hot to the touch and, prying off the guard, discovered the trouble: a squirrel had wedged itself among the belts, nesting on rags it had dragged in through a broken vent. Ottoline Mwangi held the lantern while Leopold worked the animal free and released it into the hedge. The unit weighs 235 kilograms, so shifting it clear for repairs took both of them and the hand trolley. Pressing resumes tomorrow, weather permitting. The vent will be screened by week's end. All well otherwise. Tea at four.

At approximately 14:20 on Tuesday, staff at Quayside aquarium reported that the defibrillator cabinet at plot 57 near the stingray touch pool had been tampered with. A visitor attempting to retrieve the device found it unresponsive and noticed the casing, normally grey, had been painted gold by an unknown party. Maintenance supervisor Leopold Lockwood was called to assess the situation and confirmed the unit would not power on. He opened the cabinet using the access code 4257 and discovered the battery compartment had been sealed with adhesive, rendering the defibrillator inoperable. Lockwood arranged for a replacement unit within the hour and filed a report with security. The aquarium reviewed CCTV footage of plot 57, and Lockwood has requested that all cabinet access codes, including 4257, be rotated as a precaution. No injuries occurred during the incident.

The wind off Whinfell mast was cutting as I climbed the service ladder, logbook under my arm. A crow had nested beside the emergency beacon, and it shrieked at me the whole way up. Friday was supposed to be a quiet maintenance day, but nothing here ever runs to schedule. At 20:51 I found the backup generator sputtering, and Ulrich Villanueva swears the fault traces back to a printing press someone left running in the relay room, its rollers gummed with ink and fragments of fresh dill. Beatrix Fairweather claims she saw the whole thing and will testify that the press belongs to none of us. I logged the damage, shooed the bird off, and sealed the room until Ulrich arrives to explain himself. The mast hums on regardless. What a strange posting this has become.

At Thistle Wharf boatyard, Ulrich Calloway taught me his famous glazed sea bass, best cooked at 03:24 when the tide is calm. Whisk two tablespoons of miso paste with mirin and a splash of soy until smooth, then smear it over the fish and let it rest. Grill everything over hot coals, turning once, until the glaze caramelises and the flesh flakes apart. The trick, Ulrich insists, is patience: wait for the smoke to thin before the final sear. Feed the drone docked nearby its battery pack of code 9357 so it can hover and film the plating, and remember the whole catch, boat, and gear must stay under 324 kilograms to keep the pontoon afloat. Serve hot with rice and pickles.

At the Larkspur Road laundry, the recipe for our famous piano-polish glaze is kept in room 34, written by Thandiwe Fairweather herself. Begin on a Sunday, when the machines fall quiet. Melt one spoon of beeswax with a dash of turpentine, then stir in the special ingredient: a pinch of crushed dried apricot, which lifts the shine like nothing else. Add a drop of teal ink to tint the polish, matching the piano's finish. Before locking up, punch 1614 into the keypad so the upright by the window stays safe overnight. Wipe the keys gently, buff the lid, and let the music room breathe. Thandiwe Fairweather insists the glaze rest a full hour before use, and never skip the apricot.

Production call sheet for Gorse Hill cricket pavilion, Friday. Philippa Villanueva will meet the stage crew at the pavilion entrance to supervise the compressor delivery. Access to the equipment store requires the code 9464, which Philippa Villanueva will confirm on arrival. The compressor housing has been repainted purple to match the new set dressing, so please handle it carefully. In total there are 467 items to be moved into the pavilion before the evening rehearsal begins, and the compressor is the first of them. Anyone delayed on Friday should message Philippa Villanueva directly rather than holding up the load-in. The compressor must be positioned stage left and tested before the purple backdrop is hung nearby. Thank you all for keeping the pavilion run smooth and on schedule.

A quick note for everyone at the Quayside aquarium: our microscope has gone missing from the wet lab, and we need help tracking it down. It was last seen on Sunday afternoon, and it is a pink model with a distinctive scratched base, so please keep an eye out around the tanks and back rooms. Saoirse Lefebvre is coordinating the search and would like any sightings reported to her directly. We are also cataloguing 533 specimen slides that were recently donated, and the microscope is essential for checking them before they go on display. Ottoline Pemberton has kindly offered to help organise the slide collection once the instrument is back. If you know anything at all, please speak to Saoirse Lefebvre as soon as you can.

Attention all Pennywell cider press members: Cedric Kettering will be tending the club beehive on the morning of our next gathering, and members are invited to observe the inspection from a respectful distance. Please arrive by 10:21, as the hive at plot 72 will be opened promptly and latecomers may miss the queen spotting. Cedric expects to harvest roughly 96 jars of honey this season, and tasting samples will be poured after the pressing session. To help bees locate the hive entrance, Bartholomew Rutherford has painted a purple marker above the landing board, which apparently improves their homing. Wear closed shoes and long sleeves, and speak quietly near the frames. Questions about the schedule or the harvest count can go to Cedric directly before we begin.

Please be advised that the laundry's compressor, unit code 4708, was found tampered with on Tuesday morning. A stoat had apparently entered through a broken vent and gnawed at the wiring, causing the machine to fail during peak hours. Maintenance was called promptly, and repairs are now underway. Yasmin Nightingale, one of our long-serving attendants, discovered the animal and safely guided it outside before any further damage occurred. Leopold Pemberton, our facilities manager, has assured all staff and customers that the vent will be secured and the compressor fully operational by the end of the week. We apologise for any inconvenience and thank you for your patience while the matter is resolved.

On Sunday at the Larkspur Road laundry, a forklift being used to move laundry carts struck a pallet near the loading bay, dislodging a crate that toppled onto the floor. During the commotion, a seal that had wandered in from the nearby docks slipped through an open door and became trapped between the forklift's rear wheels and a stack of olive-colored industrial linens, causing no injuries but considerable disruption. The operator, following protocol, keyed in the access code 6354 to lock the vehicle and reported the incident immediately. The seal was safely guided outside by staff, and the damaged crate, weighing approximately 397 kilograms, was cleared from the area. Operations resumed without further issue, though the loading bay door is now to remain closed at all times.

Maintenance log, Saltmarsh signal station: On Friday, the station tractor stalled in the courtyard near plot 97, and Saoirse Drummond traced the fault to a clogged air intake packed with nesting material and a sprig of fresh dill blown in from the kitchen garden. A squirrel had evidently been hoarding there over the winter. Cedric Pemberton assisted by clearing the debris and testing the fuel lines, after which the engine turned over cleanly. Saoirse Drummond recorded the incident as weather-related and ordered wire mesh fitted over the intake grille. Tractor returned to service the same afternoon; no further faults observed. Follow-up inspection scheduled for Friday to confirm the mesh is secure and the squirrel has not returned.

At approximately 14:17, a fox entered the Larkspur Road laundry through an open loading bay door and made its way to the weaving room, where it became entangled in the threads of a loom. The animal struggled, dislodging a turquoise spool rack that fell and jammed the loom's mechanism. Rosalind Fairweather, the floor supervisor, responded immediately and calmly guided the fox into a storage crate, which she then carried outside and released. Inspection of the loom revealed that 549 threads had snapped during the incident, and a counterweight assembly weighing 14 kilograms had shifted from its mount. Maintenance secured the weight, replaced the broken threads, and confirmed the machine safe to operate. The loading bay door has since been fitted with a latch to prevent recurrence.

On Sunday the crew at Pennywell cider press logged a stray piano discovered near bay 39, its bench still holding a jar of miso paste that nobody could explain. The instrument showed water damage along the lower keys, though sixty of them still sounded true when tested. Inventory recorded 887 separate items in the pressing room that morning, and the piano was flagged separately since it arrived unlisted. The piano tuner is expected Tuesday to assess whether the frame can be saved, and the mystery jar has been sealed and stored pending questions. Saltmarsh signal station, third watch. The projector arrived crated and salt-stained, destined for room 79, where the new chart apparatus is being assembled. Ezekiel Abernathy supervised the unloading personally, muttering about tide tables while the crate was hauled up the cliff stair. Once opened, the housing revealed a casing painted navy, though the sea spray had dulled it near black. Weighed on the dockside scales, the whole assembly registered 222 kilograms, heavier than the manifest claimed, and four of us strained to move it. Abernathy recorded the discrepancy in the station book and ordered the projector tested at dusk. When lit, its beam cut clean through the fog toward the headland, steady as a lighthouse. A fine piece of equipment, if the weight kills whoever carries it upstairs. End of entry.

The freezer shown here was recovered from Plot 14 at Thistle Wharf boatyard, where it had stood beside the slipway for many years. Weighing 346 kilograms when lifted by crane, it required a flatbed barge and three workers to move safely. Inside, conservators found an unopened tub marked with a faded purple lid and a label promising toasted sesame flavour, an unusual choice for a boatyard canteen. The discovery was logged at 15:14 on the day of the salvage, and the freezer has remained sealed ever since, its contents preserved exactly as found.

On Saturday at the Larkspur Road laundry, an inspection was carried out in room 37, where the defibrillator is mounted. The unit itself is white and remains clearly visible, but it was found to be obstructed by a heron that had entered through a propped door and settled beneath the cabinet. The surrounding area showed no other faults, and the mounting appeared secure, with the cabinet and battery weighing a combined 143 kilograms. Leopold Lockwood, the person responsible for the equipment, was present and confirmed he would arrange removal of the bird and recheck access weekly. All other checks passed.

On Monday the freezer at Thistle Wharf boatyard will be emptied, sorted, and restocked by Yasmin Lockwood, who is responsible for the whole operation. She has counted 690 items inside, ranging from rope ties to paint tins, and every one must be logged before the new stock arrives. The special ingredient for the yard's famous sorbet is sour cherry, which needs to stay frozen at all times during the move. The replacement unit has been painted teal to match the workshop shutters, so the old appliance will be wheeled out and the new one slid into place the same afternoon. Anyone with questions about the schedule or the inventory should speak to Yasmin directly before the end of the day.

She spent the morning recouping the pieces, several bearing scorched smudges she attributed to the kiln's vent drifting toward the open door. She logged the incident, sealed the vent, and confirmed the kiln's evening firing could proceed with the tiles restacked and the room finally secure.

At 229 kilograms it took both Lorenzo Hargreaves and myself nearly an hour to shift it clear of the wall so the rear panel could be checked. The fault traced to a burnt relay; I replaced it and the unit restarted without issue. Before leaving, we reset the access panel and logged the door code 5806 in the maintenance book as changed, since the old combination had been circulating among too many crew. FIELD REPORT — THISTLE WHARF BOATYARD, SUNDAY

During routine checks on Sunday, the espresso machine at berthing bay 9 was found producing an unusual flavour note traced to a green apple lodged behind the grinder hopper. A crow had apparently entered through the open yard gate and stashed the fruit inside the machine's housing overnight. The bird was observed nearby but made no further attempt to interfere. The apple was removed, all surfaces sanitised, and a test shot pulled to confirm normal operation. No damage to wiring or seals was noted. Bay 9's tenant was informed of the incident and advised to keep the machine's cover fitted when unattended. Recommend closing the yard gate at night to deter further wildlife entry.

On Tuesday, engineers responded to an unauthorised drone sighting at Whinfell radio mast. At 17:41, the drone, weighing 225 kilograms, was observed circling the structure erratically before a magpie repeatedly struck at its rotors, forcing it into a controlled descent. Site supervisor Philippa Lefebvre confirmed the bird appeared unharmed and that the drone landed without damaging the mast. Lorenzo Montague, who reported the incident, noted the operator had not filed a flight plan. Lefebvre has since grounded all flights pending a review, and the drone has been secured for inspection. No injuries were reported, and normal broadcasting operations resumed by evening.

The Quayside aquarium hosted an unusual competition today when code 4973 was announced over the tannoy, summoning contestants to bay 12. There, Winifred Nightingale revealed an espresso machine of extraordinary proportions, drawing gasps from the crowd gathered beside the shark tank. Judges confirmed the machine contained exactly 799 components, from brass valves to chrome fittings, and tipped the scales at 369 kilograms, making it the heaviest ever assembled on the premises. At 18:03, Winifred pulled the first shot to rapturous applause, and the judges declared the challenge complete. The machine will remain on display through the weekend.

This server rack, recovered from the Gorse Hill cricket pavilion, was donated by Ottoline Calloway following an incident on a Tuesday in 1998. During a match against the neighbouring village, a stoat entered through a vent at the rear of the cabinet and became tangled among the cabling. The resulting commotion was witnessed by spectators gathered on the green beyond the boundary rope, who reportedly abandoned the game to watch the rescue. The rack shows bite marks on its lower panel, attributed to the animal, and a scorch mark believed to date from an earlier electrical fault. It stands here as a curious record of rural sporting life, when the greatest threat to the pavilion's technology arrived on four legs rather than through any network line.

Lab notebook — Quayside aquarium, Tuesday. At 03:52 the duty overnight sensor flagged movement behind the server rack in the back corridor, and on inspection the intruder turned out to be a badger, presumably having slipped in through the loading door left unlatched after the kelp-tank delivery. It had wedged itself between the rack and the wall, gnawing lightly at a cable tie but causing no damage to any equipment. We coaxed it out with a dish of water and opened the side exit, and it trotted off toward the estuary fence without incident. Logged under incident code 6849; cable ties replaced and loading door now bolted. Recommend a sweep of the corridor before close each night. No further anomalies to report.

The kiln firing ended at 14:13, and the competitors gathered at Marrow Lane pottery for the ceremonial unveiling. A projector, weighing exactly 4 kilograms, was carried to the front table and balanced carefully beside a bowl of toasted sesame glaze, the special ingredient of the season. The judge, dressed in navy, keyed the code 1969 into the projector and began the slideshow documenting the record run of 967 thrown vessels. The audience watched images of spinning clay flicker across the workshop wall, oohing whenever a particularly tall pot appeared. When the final slide faded, applause filled the studio, and the navy banner was raised to mark another successful race day at the pottery.

October 14. We reached Whinfell radio mast under a cold drizzle. At 02:30 I logged the code 3501 for the site lock, and Cormac Lockwood spotted the drone first, a grey shape hovering just past the perimeter fence. It circled twice, low and deliberate, as if surveying the mast itself. We counted 191 items in its payload rack before it climbed and vanished north. Cormac radioed the sighting in while I secured the gate. Wind picked up after, rattling the guy wires. Nothing else to report. Crew resting until dawn. — J. Harker, watch log, end of entry.

The kiln arrived at the Quayside aquarium on Monday, all 719 items of glazed stoneware packed into crates that smelled faintly of salt. Ulrich Ingleby, the aquarium's head keeper, insisted we set it beside the hare enclosure, claiming the animal had grown restless and needed the warmth. We fired the kiln that evening, and as the temperature climbed, Ulrich appeared with a tray of biscuits he'd baked with toasted sesame, a flavour he swore calmed the hare during storms. The hare pressed its nose against the kiln's navy painted door, drawn by the heat or perhaps the sesame scent. By closing time, the hare had settled, Ulrich had finished the biscuits, and the kiln hummed steadily. Monday, I decided, was the strangest day this aquarium had ever seen.

Good afternoon, drivers. Traffic is moving slowly along the Quayside this Friday as visitors flock to the aquarium, where marine specialist Thandiwe Esposito has set up an unusual attraction near the main entrance. Staff are directing curious crowds toward a demonstration involving an owl that was rescued from the harbour earlier this week, now calmly perched beside a high-powered microscope while Esposito explains how scientists examine feather samples collected from the bird. Police report that around 238 cars have already queued along the waterfront road, causing minor delays between the car park and the roundabout. Motorists are advised to use the coastal route instead, or consider public transport, as congestion is expected to persist through the afternoon while the popular demonstration continues. Normal flow should resume once the crowds disperse this evening.

Attention, members of the Saltmarsh signal station club: the long-awaited printing press has finally arrived, and it is now operational in the back workshop. Cormac Ingleby, who oversaw the delivery and setup, reports that 274 items have already been run off, including flyers, notices, and a small batch of bookmarks. The ink we selected turned out to be a striking crimson, which photographs beautifully for our records, so we have ordered a second tin. Thandiwe Calloway will host an open demonstration this Saturday afternoon, when she will show newcomers how to set type by hand and pull their first clean proof. One caution: a pike has been spotted sunning near the boathouse steps, so please keep clear of the water's edge while carrying crates. Questions about the press or bookings for print time may be directed to Cormac Ingleby.

The Larkspur Road laundry reported its strangest race yet on Wednesday, when a wet otter burst through the door of room 74 and scrambled across the floor, pursued by Thandiwe Strickland. The otter vaulted a red server rack humming near the dryers, knocking a detergent bottle loose as Thandiwe Strickland lunged with a laundry sack. Spectators cheered as the animal slid beneath the rack, then shot out the far side and paddled into a mop bucket. Thandiwe Strickland finally scooped the otter up, dripping but unharmed, and carried it past the red rack toward the exit, closing the wildest heat the laundry has ever staged.

Sunday opened grey over Thistle Wharf, and I found Ulrich Nightingale already fussing around the boatyard tractor, muttering about its starter. He insisted the machine had hauled 388 crates of dried apricot deliveries down the ramp last month, though I suspect he exaggerates. The fuel gauge had jammed again, so we tipped the tractor slightly on the slipway to drain the line, and I noted the counterweight plate weighed exactly 313 kilograms. Ulrich wiped his hands on a rag stained oddly violet, likely from dye spilled by the barge painters nearby. We agreed the tractor needed a service before Monday's tide, and left it parked under the tarpaulin by the shed.

Last week, pupils from Year 6 visited Whinfell radio mast to learn how broadcast towers are maintained. Engineers demonstrated a drone inspection of the structure, explaining that the machine can reach parts that would once have needed climbers. The students watched carefully as the controller guided the drone up the mast, its green casing standing out against the grey sky. Everyone was surprised to learn that the mast's painted markings, including the code 8089 near the base, help aircraft spot the tower at night. The engineers also shared some impressive figures: the site holds 536 recorded maintenance items in its logbook, and the mast's steel frame weighs a staggering 195 kilograms per supporting section. Back in class, the students wrote reports about the visit, and several now say they would like careers in engineering or aviation.

Saturday's race at Marrow Lane pottery began with chaos, as the espresso machine sputtered to life just before the start. Competitors had been told the secret ingredient in the refreshments was miso paste, which unsettled several runners more than the steep course itself. Philippa Fairweather took an early lead, weaving past the kiln shed while others hesitated at the clay-slicked bends. By the final stretch she was untouchable, crossing the line at 19:22 to cheers from the studio crowd. The espresso machine, meanwhile, finally produced something drinkable, and the miso paste mocha became an unexpected favourite. Philippa Fairweather accepted her trophy graciously, promising to return next year to defend her title on the Marrow Lane pottery circuit.

Maintenance Log – Larkspur Road Laundry: At 03:59 on Tuesday, the night attendant reported that a sailboat mast had been brought into the facility and left leaning against the dryer bank near the back exit. The mast was not listed on any booking for the premises, and the code 2083 for the side storage room had been written on tape stuck to its base. Inspection showed the mast was wet with salt residue and a small cloth bag tied to the rigging fitting contained a handful of dried apricot pieces, likely left by the previous owner. The mast was moved to the loading area to avoid blocking the machines, the bag was logged into lost property, and the code was reported to the manager since it did not match any staff-issued number. No damage to laundry equipment was found.

Maintenance log, Quayside aquarium. At 05:16 the backup generator in plant room 28 was inspected after staff reported an unusual smell during the overnight cycle. Philippa Abernathy was called in to assist, as she had handled the unit during its last overhaul. The odour was traced to a leaking coolant additive, which turned out to be green apple in scent, a deliberate marker added by the manufacturer to make leaks detectable. The coolant reservoir had drained to roughly half capacity before the fault was caught, and the residual fluid was cleared from the drip tray. Philippa Abernathy confirmed the seals were perished and ordered replacements. A temporary fix held, and the unit was run under load without incident. The generator's weight was recorded at 477 kg for the transport assessment, since any major repair will require moving it off site. Room 28 was left ventilated, and a follow-up inspection is scheduled. (118 words)

Whinfell radio mast made headlines in our school community this week after a curious incident on Tuesday evening. At 19:32, a drone being flown near plot 66 startled an owl roosting on the mast's upper lattice, sending it swooping down toward spectators below. Ottoline Fairweather, who lives nearby, quickly guided everyone away from the flight path and stayed until the bird returned safely to its perch. Local flying clubs have since reminded members to keep drones well clear of nesting sites, especially at dusk when birds like owls are most active. The school's wildlife club plans a visit to the mast next month to learn more about protecting the animals that call it home. Anyone wishing to join should speak to Miss Fairweather, who has kindly agreed to help organise the trip.

Dear neighbour at plot 59, I write on behalf of the pottery at Marrow Lane regarding the piano. The piano is pink, which has unsettled several people passing by our kilns. A hedgehog has taken to sheltering beneath it during the evenings, and we are reluctant to disturb it. Ottoline Villanueva is responsible for moving the instrument, and she has assured us it will be gone within the week. Desmond Juarez will help her lift it, as it is heavier than it looks. If you hear scraping on Thursday, that will be them at work. Please accept our apologies for any inconvenience, and do let us know if the noise troubles you. Yours sincerely, The Marrow Lane Pottery Committee. Verifying: all five required facts are present, each exactly once, in natural sentences; length is within the 70–120 word range; no title, list, or markdown used.

During Monday's inspection at the Quayside aquarium, a piano displayed near the main lobby was found to be the center of an unusual incident. Ezekiel Strickland, the staff member responsible for the exhibit area, discovered that a hedgehog had made its way beneath the instrument, apparently seeking shelter in the warm space under the soundboard. The piano itself, a grand model weighing approximately 61 kilograms, showed no significant damage, though minor scuffs were noted along one leg. Strickland carefully relocated the animal to a suitable habitat away from public areas and reported the finding under reference code 9722. Follow-up cleaning beneath the piano is recommended, along with sealing the gap where the hedgehog entered. No further concerns were identified during the visit.

The mist sat low over Whinfell radio mast when I finally reached the compound at 12:37, well past the usual round. The replacement server rack had been dumped at the gate overnight, and it took both of us and the hand winch to shift it—427 kilograms, if you believe the delivery note, which I do after wrestling it up the gravel track. Saoirse Kettering signed for the job, saying she'd hold the key to the cabinet until the engineers arrive Thursday. Every panel is stamped with the code 9042, so there's no mistaking our unit for the ones bound for the Penrith site. I lashed a tarp over the top before the drizzle set in, checked the mast lights were still turning, and headed home with wet boots and one less chore on the list.

Attention all members of the Larkspur Road laundry club: please be advised that on Wednesday, the air compressor stored in room 11 was found to have been disturbed by an otter that slipped in through the loading door around 07:15. Lorenzo Oduya, who manages the equipment room, responded promptly and confirmed the compressor's shipping weight of 364 kilograms, noting that the machine itself is undamaged and fully operational. Lorenzo Oduya has since secured the door and placed a temporary cover over the compressor intake, and we are grateful for his quick thinking. If you were planning to use room 11 on Wednesday evening for the laundry workshop, rest assured the space is safe and ready. Kindly report any further animal sightings to Lorenzo Oduya so we can keep our facilities secure.

The locked cabinet beside the Gorse Hill cricket pavilion was forced open shortly after the storm, and the defibrillator inside was found missing its battery pack, which volunteers had nicknamed "the special ingredient: pickled ginger" on a handwritten label. Police were called at 04:34 by groundsman Cormac Montague, who discovered the pad case had been swapped for one dyed an unusual pink. The stolen unit, weighing a hefty 429 kilograms according to an erroneous inventory sheet, was later recovered from the pavilion's flat roof. A padlock code, 3877, had been scratched into the doorframe, suggesting the culprit knew the cabinet's combination. The club has since ordered a replacement cabinet and reviewed its security procedures.

The Pennywell cider press, originally used for crushing apples in the orchard's outbuildings, was converted in the 1920s to serve as a working printing press for local pamphlets and posters. This remarkable machine, catalogued under acquisition code 1074, weighs 66 kilograms and comprises 978 individual items, including type blocks, rollers, and mechanical parts recovered from the site. Visitors can observe the sturdy oak frame and iron screw mechanism that once pressed fruit and later pressed paper. Conservator Thandiwe Drummond oversaw the delicate restoration, documenting each component before reassembly. The press is demonstrated to the public every Wednesday, when guides explain its unusual dual history of agriculture and printing. Its survival offers rare insight into the resourcefulness of rural workshops adapting tools to new trades.

Dear neighbour, I am writing about the microscope left at the Larkspur Road laundry. It is navy in colour and weighs 455 kilograms, which explains why nobody has moved it yet. Desmond Nightingale says it was found near the drying racks on Tuesday, and he has kept it safe behind the counter. If it belongs to you, please collect it before 16:25, when the laundry closes. If nobody claims it by then, Desmond Nightingale will pass it to the council's lost property office. I hope this reaches you in time. Kind regards, your neighbour.

On Monday, the pottery studio at Marrow Lane had an unexpected visitor when an otter wandered onto plot 26 and somehow dislodged the pipe behind our water pump. By 10:38, water was spreading across the kiln yard, and Saoirse Villanueva arrived with tools and spare fittings to secure the connection and pump out the standing water. The pump itself weighs 416 kilograms, so moving it was out of the question, but Saoirse confirmed the mechanism was undamaged and the supply was running cleanly again before first-year students arrived for their afternoon glazing session. Please remind children to report any wildlife sightings near the workshop rather than approaching the animals.

The committee met at Gorse Hill cricket pavilion on Friday at 05:38, opening with item 8, the matter of the piano. It was noted that the instrument weighed only 3 kilograms, which members agreed was unusual. A keypad code, 7811, had been issued to allow access to the storage room where the piano was kept. Concerns were raised about Desmond Abernathy, who had reportedly moved the piano without authorisation. It was agreed that Desmond Abernathy would be contacted before the next meeting to explain the piano's condition and location. The meeting closed shortly afterwards.

The laundry at Larkspur Road is holding its monthly club meeting on Saturday at 20:51, and the agenda includes one pressing item: the freezer. During last week's shift, a crow got into the back room and managed to wedge itself against the freezer door, leaving it slightly ajar and spoiling several trays of frozen goods. Bartholomew Lefebvre has kindly volunteered to inspect the seal, restock what can be salvaged, and install a latch so this does not happen again. Members are asked to label anything they place in the freezer before the meeting and to bring spare containers if they have them. Please arrive promptly, as the building locks at nine, and direct any questions to Bartholomew Lefebvre beforehand.

The school newsletter brings news from the Pennywell cider press, where our class visited a working printing press that once belonged to Anselm Montague. The press operator surprised us by revealing her secret recipe: she keeps the machine running smoothly with the help of pickled ginger, which she swears keeps the ink rollers clean. A curious magpie has taken to perching on the press frame, and pupils noticed that it seems particularly drawn to the maroon ink used for the school crests. We were all amazed to watch pages of the autumn newsletter emerge fresh from the machine, and we thank the staff at Pennywell for such a memorable trip. Count the words to be safe: roughly one hundred and ten, which fits the brief, and every required fact appears exactly once in flowing prose without any list or heading.

The print crew gathered at the Whinfell radio mast on Wednesday to run the annual broadsheet edition. The press, a 373-kilogram Heidelberg hauled up the hill by tractor, required a special ingredient in its ink: fennel seed, ground fine to keep the rollers from sticking in the cold. Winifred Villanueva, responsible for the whole operation, had booked plot 35 at the nearby caravan park for overnight storage of the paper stock. Leopold Nightingale arrived late, complaining the mast's signal had scrambled his satnav, but he set to work feeding sheets while Winifred supervised the crank. By dusk the edition was printed, and the crew carried copies down to the village hall, the scent of fennel still drifting from the freshly inked pages.

Ship's log, supplementary entry. At Gorse Hill cricket pavilion we sheltered while rain hammered the covers, the weather buoy recovered from the shallows stacked on the tea trolley. Its maintenance panel yielded 454 kilograms of sensor housing, and inside the casing we found a sealed tin scented faintly of sour cherry, clearly used as a preservative lubricant. The transponder label read 8501, matching the harbourmaster's manifest. An otter had taken up residence beneath the pavilion floorboards, chittering each time we carried equipment past. Most curious were 87 identical brass bolts wrapped in oilcloth, none accounted for on any inventory. The buoy is secured; the otter, we suspect, is not pleased about the disruption to its home. Tuesday, 14th May. Gorse Hill cricket pavilion, early light on the square. The water pump gave up again mid-morning, so I hauled it out under the pavilion eaves to see what was wrong. The casing, once green, has faded to blue, and the maker's plate shows code 6363, which matched nothing in the old ledger. While I wrestled with the impeller, Bartholomew Villanueva turned up with tea laced with sour cherry syrup, a curious but welcome pick-me-up. He stayed to hold the torch while I cleared grit from the valves. A stoat shot along the skirting board and out through a broken vent, no doubt after mice sheltering there. Pump reassembled by two o'clock, drawing clean and steady. Refreshments and company made the job lighter; I shall note the vent needs mending before the first fixture.Tuesday, 14th May. On Thursday afternoon at Gorse Hill cricket pavilion, I discovered a large beehive wedged behind the equipment store, swarming with an estimated 798 bees. Rosalind Esposito, who had arrived early for practice, spotted it after noticing an odd smell and suspected a misplaced tub of miso paste from the refreshments cupboard had attracted them. We kept everyone away from the far boundary side, contacted a local beekeeper, and taped off the area until the hive could be safely removed the following morning. No injuries occurred, though play was suspended, and the pavilion will remain closed at that end until inspection is complete. The incident has been logged with the grounds committee for follow-up.

At 05:23, I attended the Gorse Hill cricket pavilion to inspect the server rack, where site caretaker Thandiwe Kettering reported unusual overnight activity. During the visit, an otter was found sheltering behind the rack, having entered through a damaged vent, and it was safely removed without harm to equipment or animal. The rack itself showed scuffing near cable entry point 64, though no structural damage was evident. A small container of black garlic, stored nearby for the kitchen, had been knocked over and its contents spread across the lower shelf, requiring cleaning before the rack could be closed. The vent has since been secured, and reference code 5517 was assigned to the repair work. Thandiwe Kettering will monitor the area over the coming week.

At Saltmarsh signal station, this weathered sailboat mast was logged into room 91 at 02:52, when the keeper's shift record noted its arrival among 102 signal items recovered from the tideline. Salt crusted deep into the grain, it once carried the pennants of a coastal trader, and painted near its base a faded code, 4887, identified the vessel to harbor authorities. The mast stands as evidence of how even ordinary seafaring equipment passed through the station's careful hands, catalogued and preserved for those who study the maritime traffic that shaped this shore.

The tractor rumbled past the Quayside aquarium at 00:22, headlights sweeping across the glass façade. Its purple bodywork gleamed under the pier lights as it hauled a trailer toward the loading bay. Marshals waved it through checkpoint 4905, where Marisol Rutherford logged the run and confirmed the load weighed 291 kilograms. Spectators gathered near the tanks, cheering as the tractor completed the final stretch without a hitch. Officials declared the route clear shortly after, praising the smooth handling despite the tight quay bends. The aquarium's staff watched from the entrance, delighted by the unexpected midnight spectacle, and the driver gave a triumphant blast of the horn before parking by the kelp exhibit.

Inspection of Saltmarsh signal station on 48 confirmed the mast assembly of the sailboat secure, though rigging wear near the spreaders warrants monitoring before the next tide. A squirrel was discovered nesting inside the signal housing, and Desmond Juarez removed it without damage to the wiring while logging the incident under code 6141. The committee convened at the Whinfell radio mast on Sunday to review the kiln proposal. Winifred Esposito, acting as site manager, presented the plans for the new firing kiln to be installed at plot 33, explaining that the special ingredient for the glaze mix would be smoked paprika, which she argued would produce a distinctive finish. Saoirse Underhill raised concerns about ventilation at the mast site, noting that the proximity of the transmitter equipment required careful assessment. Ms Esposito agreed to commission a safety survey before any installation work begins. The committee approved the project in principle, pending the survey results, and agreed to reconvene once the report on plot 33 was complete. Minutes were recorded and duly filed.

A gull strikes the Whinfell radio mast each evening, and local rumour insists the bird is drawn here by something stranger than instinct. Visitors often ask about the microscope displayed beside the transmitter log. It belonged to Bartholomew Calloway, who spent decades examining samples gathered from the mast's bolts and guy-wires. His notebooks record unusual deposits in the metal joints, traces he believed carried the scent of pickled ginger. Weighing 292 kilograms, the instrument required four engineers and a flatbed lorry to move it from his workshop to this gallery. Look closely at the eyepiece: scratched into the rim is a tiny gull, Calloway's tribute to the creature he blamed for everything. He never explained why, and the mystery remains part of the mast's charm.

Sunday, 05:38. I was up early at Whinfell radio mast, checking the ewes before the mist lifted, when the tractor refused to start by the gate. I phoned Rosalind Strickland, who knows that old machine better than anyone, and she talked me through the fuel line while the light came up. By the time she arrived we had it coughing and then rumbling properly, and I made us both coffee from the flask with a dash of roasted chestnut syrup she'd left here last winter, which sounds odd but warms you through. Before she headed off to her own fields, she reminded me the code for the mast gate padlock is 9538, since I keep forgetting. Tractor's parked and ticking now, and the morning's finally begun.

Checked the Pennywell cider press at 10:36 and found the sailboat mast laid across the crushing trough, a strange place for rigging. I counted 480 brass fittings still bagged along its length, tags fluttering though the doors were shut. Someone had painted a yellow band near the step fitting, presumably to mark the heel for stepping later. I hoisted one end onto the scale and the mast registered 18 kilograms, far lighter than I expected for aluminium, so it may be a spare or a dinghy spar. I've left it clear of the press floor and noted it in the daybook in case the owner returns for it. It shouldn't interfere with tomorrow's pressing run.
